concepts.name: Entra ID group claims and the groups overage
Responding to a secret committed to git

questions.prompt: Your API authorises by checking the `groups` claim in Entra ID JWT access tokens. A user in 230 security groups is denied on every group-protected endpoint, while colleagues in 40 groups are fine. Why?

choices.text: Entra ID keeps just the first 200 groups, and the ones you need were cut from the list
The token grew too large, so Entra ID quietly issued an ID token in its place
Group claims only appear in SAML tokens, so a JWT never carries group membership
Past 200 groups the token has no `groups` claim, only an overage claim to follow

questions.explanation: To keep tokens within header size limits, Entra ID includes at most 200 groups in a JWT (150 in SAML). Above that it omits the `groups` claim entirely and adds an overage indicator (`_claim_names` / `_claim_sources`, or `hasgroups` in the implicit flow), and the app must read membership from Microsoft Graph. It doesn't truncate the list. Emitting only groups assigned to the app, or using app roles, avoids the problem.

sources.title: Access token claims reference - Microsoft identity platform
sources.claim: If a user is in more groups than the overage limit (200 for JWT, 150 for SAML), Entra ID doesn't emit the groups claim and adds an overage claim telling the app to query Microsoft Graph for group membership.

sources.title: Configure group claims and app roles in tokens
sources.claim: When the user is in too many groups there are no groups in the token; the app must detect the overage claim and call Microsoft Graph; selecting groups assigned to the application or using app roles avoids the overage.

questions.prompt: An attacker copies a DPoP-bound access token from a log file and replays it to your API from their own machine. Why does a correctly implemented API reject the call?

choices.text: DPoP tokens are encrypted for one IP address, so other machines can't use them
Its `cnf.jkt` ties it to the client's key, and the attacker can't sign a proof
Each DPoP token is single use, so the server marks it spent after the first call
The API sends every request to the authorisation server's revocation endpoint

questions.explanation: DPoP binds a token to the client's public key: the token carries a `cnf` claim with the key's thumbprint (`jkt`), and every request must include a DPoP proof JWT signed with the matching private key, covering the method, URL and a hash of the token. Without the private key the attacker can't produce a valid proof. DPoP doesn't bind tokens to IP addresses, and the token itself is reused across requests.

sources.title: RFC 9449: OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)
sources.claim: DPoP sender-constrains tokens: the access token is bound via a cnf claim holding the JWK SHA-256 thumbprint (jkt) of the client's key, and each request carries a DPoP proof JWT signed with the private key, with htm, htu, iat, jti and ath; the resource server checks the proof and that its key matches the token binding.

questions.prompt: An hour ago a developer pushed a commit containing a production database connection string to your GitHub repository. What do you do, in what order, and why isn't deleting the commit enough?

model_answer.summary: Revoke or rotate the secret first, because that makes the leaked value useless; then clean history, knowing copies survive elsewhere, and add push protection so it doesn't happen again.
key_points: First revoke or rotate the credential (new password or key, updated in Key Vault or config), since a revoked secret is useless to anyone who copied it
Deleting or rewriting the commit isn't enough: the value survives in clones, forks, pull requests that reference it and GitHub's cached views

If you rewrite history (for example `git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal`), expect side effects such as changed commit hashes and recontamination, and ask GitHub Support to remove cached views and affected pull request refs
Prevent a repeat with secret scanning push protection, which blocks pushes containing detected secrets before they reach the repository

questions.explanation: The tempting answer is to force-push a cleaned history and move on. But the secret was public for an hour, and other copies are beyond your control, so only rotating it closes the hole. History cleanup is optional hygiene; prevention is push protection plus keeping secrets out of code.

sources.title: Removing sensitive data from a repository
sources.claim: If the sensitive data is a secret, first revoke or rotate it; rewriting history doesn't remove it from clones, forks, cached views or pull requests; history rewrites have side effects such as changed hashes and recontamination; GitHub Support can remove cached views and dereference affected PRs.

sources.title: About push protection
sources.claim: Push protection blocks pushes that contain detected secrets before they reach the repository, whereas secret scanning alerts find secrets already committed.

questions.prompt: Your app needs only three Entra ID groups for authorisation, but many users belong to hundreds of groups. Which configuration avoids the groups overage, per Microsoft's guidance?

choices.text: Request the `groups` claim in the ID token as well, since ID tokens have no limit
Define app roles, assign the three groups to them, and check the `roles` claim
Switch the app to SAML, since SAML tokens can carry more groups than a JWT can
Raise the token size limit in the app registration so all groups always fit in

questions.explanation: Microsoft suggests two ways around the overage: emit only the groups assigned to the application, or define app roles that allow users and groups, assign the groups to them, and authorise on the `roles` claim, which also saves mapping group IDs to meanings. ID tokens are subject to the same limits, SAML's limit is lower (150), and there is no token-size setting to raise.

sources.title: Configure group claims and app roles in tokens
sources.claim: Group claim limits are 200 for JWT, 150 for SAML and 6 for the implicit flow; to avoid the overage select 'Groups assigned to the application' or define app roles allowing users and groups, which puts a roles claim in the token.

questions.prompt: Which threat does RFC 9449 say DPoP can't defend against?

choices.text: A stolen access token replayed from another machine without the key
A leaked DPoP-bound refresh token redeemed by someone lacking the key
A captured proof replayed on a different URL than the one it was for
Script injected into the SPA that uses the key to make new proofs

questions.explanation: If attacker code runs inside the client, it can use the client's key to create DPoP proofs, and the RFC says there is most likely no feasible defence beyond preventing XSS; server nonces only limit pre-generated proofs. The other three are what DPoP is for: tokens are useless without the private key, and each proof covers a specific HTTP method and URL.

sources.title: RFC 9449: OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)
sources.claim: DPoP binds access and refresh tokens to a key and each proof to the request's method and URI, but an attacker running code in the client (for example via XSS) can create proofs, with most likely no feasible defence except preventing XSS.

questions.prompt: A teammate committed an API key, then pushed a second commit that deletes it. According to GitHub's guidance, what should happen first?

choices.text: Revoke or rotate the key; it's still in history, forks and clones
Nothing more: the latest commit removed it, so nobody can read the key
Force-push a rewritten history; after that, keeping the key is safe
Make the repository private, which removes the key from forks as well

questions.explanation: A later commit only hides the key from the latest version; it stays in the history, and possibly in clones, forks, pull requests and cached views. GitHub's first step for a leaked secret is to revoke or rotate it, which can resolve the issue without rewriting history at all. A rewrite doesn't reach other people's clones or forks.

sources.title: Removing sensitive data from a repository
sources.claim: For a committed secret the first step is to revoke or rotate it; data stays in clones, forks, cached views and pull requests even after a history rewrite.

questions.prompt: An hour ago a developer pushed a commit containing a production database connection string to your GitHub repository. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Revoke or rotate the credential first, so a copy of the leaked value is useless
A history rewrite leaves the secret in other clones, forks and cached views
Push protection can block pushes with detected secrets before they reach the repo
Force-pushing a rewritten history removes the secret everywhere it was copied
Rewriting history keeps every commit hash, so open clones keep working as before

questions.explanation: GitHub's first step for a leaked secret is to revoke or rotate it, which makes it useless even to someone who already copied it. Rewriting history, for example with `git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal`, doesn't reach other people's clones and forks, GitHub's cached views or pull request refs, and it changes commit hashes and risks recontamination when an old clone pushes again. Push protection prevents a repeat by blocking pushes that contain detected secrets before they reach the repository.

sources.title: Removing sensitive data from a repository
sources.claim: If the sensitive data is a secret, first revoke or rotate it; after rewriting history the data still persists in clones and forks, cached views and pull request references; rewriting changes commit hashes and risks recontamination from old clones; GitHub Support can remove cached views and dereference pull requests.

sources.title: About push protection
sources.claim: Push protection prevents hardcoded secrets from being pushed by blocking pushes before they reach the repository, whereas secret scanning alerts report leaks that have already happened.
